questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the key difference between a notebook experiment and a production ML pipeline?
options: A notebook experiment always produces a less accurate model than a pipeline
A pipeline is a repeatable, automated, versioned sequence of stages that can be re-run, while a notebook experiment is a manual, one-off result
Notebooks cannot be used at any point in a real MLOps workflow
A pipeline only runs once, while a notebook experiment can be re-run indefinitely
questions.explain: MLOps turns a one-off manual notebook result into a repeatable, automated, versioned pipeline that can run again on new data, on a schedule, or on demand.

questions.q: What happens in the data preparation stage of the ML lifecycle?
options: Raw data is pulled, cleaned, validated against an expected schema, and split into training/validation/test sets, as automated code rather than a manual export
The model's hyperparameters are tuned to maximize test accuracy
The trained model is rolled out behind a serving endpoint with canary traffic
Live production predictions are compared against the original training distribution
questions.explain: Data preparation turns raw data into training-ready data through automated cleaning, schema validation, and splitting — done as code so it reproduces identically on the next run.

questions.q: What role does an evaluation gate play in the ML lifecycle?
options: It automatically deploys any model that finishes training without further checks
It replaces the need for a model registry entirely
It decides whether a newly trained model is allowed to move forward, by comparing its metric score against the current production model or a fixed minimum bar
It only applies to GPU-trained models, never CPU-trained ones
questions.explain: The evaluation stage scores a model against held-out data and checks that score against a gate — the deployed model's score or a fixed bar — before allowing promotion.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say deployment is 'never the end of the story' for a model, unlike many stable application deployments?
options: Because models must be redeployed every single day regardless of performance
Because model deployments never use the same rollout patterns (canary, blue/green) as application deployments
Because deployment infrastructure for models is fundamentally incompatible with Kubernetes
Because a live model's job is to stay accurate against real-world data that keeps changing, so it must be monitored continuously after deployment
questions.explain: A model deployment isn't a finish line — the real world keeps changing underneath a live model, so its accuracy must be continuously monitored, unlike many application deployments that stay correct once shipped.

questions.q: What does the monitoring stage feed back into, and why does that matter?
options: It feeds back into the evaluation stage only, skipping data preparation entirely
It feeds back into data preparation, triggering a fresh data pull and retrain when drift is detected — which is what makes this a lifecycle rather than a one-time project
It feeds forward into deployment, bypassing training on every retrain
It does not feed back anywhere; monitoring is the final stage with no further action
questions.explain: A drift alert from monitoring loops back to stage 1 (data preparation), triggering retraining — that feedback loop is what makes the five stages a lifecycle instead of a linear, one-time process.
